speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Could you please describe the onset of your gait and limb ataxia—did it begin suddenly or gradually, and have you experienced any associated symptoms like slurred speech or swallowing difficulties?

speaker: Patient
text: I started having trouble walking recently, and people say I look drunk when I walk. I also feel clumsy in my arms and legs, especially on the right side.

speaker: Doctor
text: Is this the first time you've experienced these symptoms, or have you had similar episodes in the past? I also need to know if you have a history of alcohol abuse, diabetes, or any autoimmune conditions.

speaker: Patient
text: I have Crohn disease and it has been difficult to control. I have been taking natalizumab for about a year.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you have any visual changes, such as double vision or loss of vision in one eye, or any numbness or tingling in your extremities? Have you noticed any bladder or bowel dysfunction recently?

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had a recent fever or major infection that I know of. The symptoms are mostly gait imbalance, limb ataxia, and weaker use of my right arm.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your history of Crohn's disease and natalizumab use, I am concerned about the possibility of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). REQUEST TEST: Brain MRI with contrast.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: MRI Brain shows lesions consistent with Progressive Multifocal Encephalopathy (PML). T1/T2 images demonstrate multifocal demyelinating lesions without gadolinium enhancement, indicative of PML.

speaker: Patient
text: The walking difficulty and coordination problems are the main issues. I do not have chest pain or other major symptoms besides the neurological problems. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Multiple sclerosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: The previous doctor's assessment of Multiple Sclerosis is unlikely given your specific symptoms and natalizumab history, which strongly points toward Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy.
